Exploring the unique symptom manifestations and conceptualizations of depression among South Asian diaspora populations in Western countries is essential for equitable psychiatric care. Methods: We conducted a qualitative and mixed-methods clinical investigation among adult diaspora members of South Asian heritage (including individuals of Indian, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi descent) living in English-speaking nations who presented with clinical depression or depressive distress. In-depth semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted to elicit detailed personal symptom narratives and illness perceptions. Reported emotional, cognitive, and bodily symptoms were systematically documented, categorized, and compared against standard ICD-11 diagnostic criteria for depressive episodes, while accounting for acculturation level and migration history. Results: Participants articulated depression predominantly through somatic idioms of distress, including persistent physical exhaustion, generalized bodily aches, chest tightness, and emotional heartache, alongside classical depressive symptoms of low mood and cognitive fatigue. Qualitative analysis identified significant cultural stigma, interpersonal tensions, and family duty pressures as key mediators shaping symptom presentation and healthcare-seeking behaviors. Conclusions: Depressive illness among the South Asian diaspora frequently incorporates prominent somatic symptom idioms alongside affective distress, highlighting the need for culturally adapted clinical assessments aligning with ICD-11 diagnostic frameworks.
